en: The Wave of Bliss (Ānandalaharī)

O Bhavānī, even the Lord of Creatures, the destroyer of Tripura, is not able to praise you with his four faces; nor is the Commander of the Army with his five; nor even the Lord of Serpents with his thousand mouths. Tell me, then, what opportunity can there be for others in this matter? 1.
The sweetness of ghee, milk, grapes, and honey cannot be described by any words as something distinct; it remains an object of experience solely for the tongue.
Likewise, how can we describe Your supreme beauty, which is an object of perception solely for the eye of Śiva, and whose qualities lie beyond the reach of all the Vedas?
In your mouth is betel, in your pair of eyes is a smear of collyrium, on your forehead shines saffron, and around your neck is a string of pearls;
with a shimmering girdle and a golden garment upon your broad hips, I worship you, Gaurī, the youthful consort of the Lord of Mountains, without ceasing. 3.

Victorious is the goddess Satī, the daughter of Mātanga, whose slender-limbed form possesses a graceful gait; she shines with earrings that quiver upon hearing the sound of the lute flowing from the slopes of her breasts, which are like the great clusters of blossoms on the radiant Mandāra tree, and her eyes are as sweet as lotuses to Lord Śambhu. 4.

May my fair-faced Aparṇā, whose limbs are encircled by ornaments of jewels and gold shining like the new sun; who has accepted Śiva as her own, her body and beautiful eyes resembling a doe; who is as yellow as lightning and made lovely by a golden waist-belt; remain full for me with boundless happiness. 5.
Born from the Himalaya mountain, with graceful hands adorned with sprouts, bearing beautiful flowers of pearls and a mass of hair like bees;

established upon the pillar of the body, bent by the fruit of her breasts, and rich with the essence of eloquent speech—this creeper of the bliss of consciousness shines forth, destroying all maladies. (6)
Others here respectfully resort to a creeper that possesses leaves and is endowed with a few virtues; but my mind shines thus:
only the leafless one (Aparṇā) is to be served by all in this world, for it is she, surrounded by whom, even the ancient Sthāṇu (Śiva) indeed bestows the state of absolute liberation.

You are the ordainer of all dharmas, you are the mother who gives birth to all objects of purpose, and you are the root whose lotus feet are worshipped by Kubera; you are the origin of all desires, O Mother who have conquered Kāmadeva, and you are the seed of liberation for the virtuous—the queen of the Supreme Brahman. (8)
Although your devotion toward me is great, I am one whose mind is unshakable; nevertheless, O illustrious lady, you must now look upon me with compassion.
A cloud bestows sweet water into the mouth of the cātaka bird; I suspect by what means has my own mind been so entreated? (9)
Quickly bestow the glance of your compassionate side upon me, whose conduct is virtuous; it is not fitting for you to remain indifferent toward me, who have entered into the vow of seeking refuge.
Otherwise, alas, how could the wish-fulfilling creeper differ from ordinary vines and other common plants if it did not grant one's desires immediately?
O Umā, having placed my entire trust in the pair of your lotus feet, I have not resorted to any other deity here;
yet, O Mother of Lambodara, if your heart does not become compassionate toward me, who shall I seek for refuge when I am left without support? 11.

Just as iron, upon contact with fire, instantly attains the state of gold, and just as the path of a street becomes pure when joined by the current of the Gaṅgā, so too, if my inner self, though exceedingly defiled by various sins, is attached to You with love, how could it not become stainless? 12.
"There is no certainty that one will obtain the fruit desired from anyone other than you; you alone are capable of bestowing even more than what is desired by the ignorant.

Thus have the ancients, beginning with the lotus-born Brahmā, declared. O Sovereign Lady, therefore, ensure that the minds of those devoted to you remain attached to you day and night, as is fitting. 13.

Victorious is your radiant palace, O Queen of the Great King of the Three Worlds, which bears your own form reflected in walls made of shimmering various gems and crystal, whose roof-peak is a mansion for the flickering crescent moon, and which is attended by a retinue including Mukunda, Brahmā, Indra, and others. 14.

O Daughter of the Lord of Mountains, Maheśa is your lord of life; his residence is on Kailāsa; Brahmā, Indra, and the other gods offer him praise; the entire universe is his family; and the multitude of Siddhas stands with palms joined in supplication. There is not even the slightest comparison anywhere for your good fortune. (15)

An aged bull is his vehicle; irregular food is his diet; a cremation ground is his dwelling; a multitude of serpents is his playground; and the act of adorning himself with snakes is his mode of ornamentation.
O Mother, this entire array of requisites for the enemy of Smara is well known in the world, yet the majesty of your good fortune lies in the fact that he possesses such sovereignty. 16.

O auspicious lady, I consider that Paśupati—who possesses an innate disposition for the rite of universal dissolution, who sits in cremation grounds, and who has smeared himself with ashes—wore the Hālāhala poison around his neck out of compassion for the entire earth; indeed, I perceive this as the fruit of association with you. 17.
O Daughter of the Mountain, seeing your unsurpassed beauty, Gaṅgā became water-bodied out of supreme fear;
therefore, O Lord of the Mountain, out of compassion, you have established her upon your own head by dwelling there, beholding her lotus-like face. (18)
O Blessed One, taking up the water from your bath— anointing liquid mixed with abundant sandalwood paste, musk,
saffron, and flowers— the Creator gathers the dust from your moving feet with his own hands and fashions the creation of those whose eyes are like the lotuses of the gods.

He who remembers you playing with your friends in a lake filled with blossoming creepers during the joyful spring, graced by rows of ruddy geese amidst shimmering lotuses, its waters stirred by the Malaya breeze—for him, the torment born of fever shall depart. (20)
The Ānandalaharī is complete.
